docs.title: Focus Pulse
docs.text:
A Chrome extension that measures how you actually spend your browsing time, and keeps every measurement on your own machine.

Most productivity tools ask you to create an account and then quietly ship your browsing history to a server. Focus Pulse does the opposite. It watches which site is in your active tab, how long it stays there, and how often you switch — then turns that into a daily focus score you can look at. Nothing is uploaded, because there is nowhere to upload it to.

0network requests made by the extension 0third parties with access to your data Noaccount, login, or cloud sync Localstorage only, erased when you uninstall

Add to Chrome Installation options Read the privacy policy

Focus Pulse is available on the Chrome Web Store, or you can load it unpacked straight from the repository.

docs.title: What it measures
docs.text:
Time per site. Whenever a tab is focused and you are actually at the computer, the time is credited to that site's hostname — wikipedia.org, not the full address of the page you were reading.

Tab switching. Every switch between tabs is counted. Frequent switching is the clearest signal of fragmented attention, and it is the largest term in the focus score.

Short visits. Sessions that end almost as soon as they begin get counted separately. Ten seconds on a site, then away again, is a different behaviour from ten minutes of reading.

Tab load. The highest number of tabs you had open simultaneously that day.

docs.title: What it shows you
docs.text:
Surface What you get Popup Today's focus score on a gauge, top sites, live tab count, export buttons Dashboard Focus score, personal baseline, insights, browsing statistics, selectable 7-day, 15-day and 30-day trends, Bar Graph and Line Graph views, history, top sites and weekly reports Exports Statistics as JSON or CSV, plus a plain-text weekly report

The score is translated into a letter grade from A to D and a focus zone — highly focused, moderately focused, or distracted. The exact formula is documented in How it works, because a score you can't interrogate isn't worth much.

docs.title: Designed to be honest about time
docs.text:
A focus tracker that counts time you weren't there is worse than no tracker at all. Focus Pulse stops the clock when the system goes idle or the screen locks, and pauses when the browser window loses focus.

It also makes one deliberate exception: if the active tab is playing audio, you are treated as present even without keyboard or mouse input. Watching a 40-minute talk should not be recorded as 40 minutes of idling.

Built for Manifest V3

Chrome suspends extension service workers aggressively. Focus Pulse checkpoints the session in progress once a minute so that long stretches on a single page survive suspension instead of vanishing from your statistics.

docs.title: Privacy in one line
docs.text: Your browsing statistics are written to your browser's local extension storage and stay there until you delete them or uninstall the extension. The full policy is on the Privacy page.

The submission-ready build. Scoring was centralised so the popup, dashboard, and weekly report can no longer disagree with each other, and the tracking worker was hardened against Manifest V3's aggressive suspension.

20 August 2026

  • Renamed the product from Focus Tracker to Focus Pulse. The extension name, in-app labels, exported filenames, and weekly report header all use the new name. The repository and documentation URLs keep their original browser-focus-tracker slug so existing links and the published privacy policy URL stay valid.
  • Revised the score-to-grade scale.

13 August 2026

  • Fixed dashboard styling and the weekly report download.
  • Fixed the success notification on JSON export.
  • Centralised scoring logic in utils.js and made the dashboard defensive against missing or partial data.
  • Cleaned up the background service worker: serialised all storage read-modify-write operations behind a queue to prevent lost updates, and made the auto-save alarm await its write so Chrome cannot suspend the worker mid-save.
  • Finalised project documentation.

docs.title: Planned
docs.text:
Ideas under consideration, from the project README:

  • Custom productivity goals and monthly reports.
  • Website categorisation.
  • Focus session reminders.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A score you can't interrogate isn't worth much. This page documents exactly what Focus Pulse measures, what it deliberately refuses to measure, and how the number on the gauge is calculated.

docs.title: What counts as browsing time
docs.text:
Time is credited to a site only when all three of these hold:

  • The site's tab is the active tab in its window.
  • A Chrome window actually has focus.
  • The system is not idle or locked.

The moment any of those stops being true, the clock stops and the elapsed time is banked against that site's hostname. When they become true again, a fresh session starts.

docs.title: Pages that are never tracked
docs.text: Internal browser pages are skipped entirely — chrome://, chrome-extension://, edge://, and about:. Time spent on the new tab page or in browser settings is not counted as browsing and never appears in your statistics.

docs.title: Hostnames, not URLs
docs.text: Only the hostname is stored. Reading three different articles on wikipedia.org produces one entry, wikipedia.org, with the combined time. The full address is used momentarily to extract that hostname and is not retained.

docs.title: Handling absence honestly
docs.text:
The hardest part of a focus tracker is not counting time you weren't there for.

Idle detection runs on a 5-minute threshold. Chrome's idle API only sees physical keyboard and mouse input, so a shorter threshold could punish normal behaviour — reading a long article without touching the mouse would register as absence. Five minutes is the trade-off: genuine idle time can take up to five minutes to be noticed, while ordinary reading is less likely to be misclassified.

Audio is treated as presence. If the active tab is playing audio when the system goes idle, tracking continues. Watching a 40-minute talk is engagement, not idling. A locked screen has no such exemption — if you locked the computer, tracking stops.

Brief focus loss has a 300 ms grace period. Opening DevTools or a zoom menu can momentarily unfocus the window. Focus Pulse waits 300 ms and re-checks before deciding the browser genuinely lost focus, so these brief interruptions do not unnecessarily fragment tracking.

Surviving Manifest V3

Chrome can suspend extension service workers, and in-memory variables can disappear with them. Focus Pulse treats chrome.storage.local as the persistent source of truth and runs a one-minute alarm that checkpoints the session in progress. Without that checkpoint, a long single-tab session — such as a video or long read — could lose time when the service worker is suspended.

docs.title: Short visits
docs.text:
A session shorter than 10 seconds is recorded as a short visit and can reduce the focus score.

A short visit is only counted when the session ends because you deliberately moved away from the page — for example, by switching tabs or loading a new URL.

A session cut short because the browser lost focus, the system went idle, or the session was checkpointed by the alarm is not treated as a short visit. Those events are interruptions outside the browsing behaviour being measured.

docs.title: The focus score
docs.text:
Every day starts at 100 points. The score then loses points for selected browsing behaviours:

score = 100

       − (tab switches × 1.5)
       − (short visits × 3)
       − (10 if more than 15 distinct sites were visited)

final score = clamped to 0–100 and rounded

docs.title: Grades and focus zones
docs.text:
The final score is also shown as a letter grade and a focus zone.

Score Grade Focus zone 90–100 A Highly focused 80–89 B Highly focused 65–79 C Moderately focused 50–64 D Moderately focused 0–49 D Distracted

The focus zone gives a simple interpretation of the score, while the letter grade provides a more detailed classification.

docs.title: Why did my score change?
docs.text:
Focus Pulse makes the score easier to understand by showing a breakdown of where points were lost.

The dashboard shows:

  • Starting score — every day begins at 100.
  • Tab switching — each tab switch reduces the score by 1.5 points.
  • Short visits — each qualifying short visit reduces the score by 3 points.
  • Website variety — visiting more than 15 distinct sites applies a 10-point penalty.
  • Today's focus score — the resulting score after the penalties are applied and the value is clamped between 0 and 100.

This breakdown is intended to make the score transparent rather than presenting it as an unexplained number.

docs.title: Your Personal Baseline
docs.text:
After enough daily data has been collected, Focus Pulse calculates a personal baseline using up to the previous seven days of focus scores.

At least three previous days are required before a baseline is shown. This prevents the comparison from being based on too little information.

The dashboard compares today's score with your usual score and shows whether you are:

  • Above your usual focus
  • Below your usual focus
  • Around your usual focus

The personal baseline is calculated entirely from your locally stored daily statistics.

docs.title: Focus Insight
docs.text:
Focus Pulse also provides a short Focus Insight based on the day's browsing statistics.

The insight can highlight patterns such as:

  • Frequent tab switching
  • Several short visits
  • A large number of different websites
  • A score significantly above or below your personal baseline
  • A generally strong or steady focus score

The insight is intended as a lightweight suggestion, not as a measurement of your actual productivity or mental attention.

For example, a high number of tab switches may result in a suggestion to keep fewer active tabs. A score above your personal baseline may result in a positive message encouraging you to continue the browsing routine that worked well.

These insights are generated locally and do not require your browsing data to be sent anywhere.

docs.title: Limitations of the score
docs.text:
The focus score is a v1 heuristic, not a scientific measurement of attention, productivity, or concentration.

The score measures observable browsing behaviour such as tab switching, short visits, and website variety. It cannot determine whether you are actually focused on a task.

For example, reading a long document without switching tabs may produce a high score even though Focus Pulse cannot know whether you were paying attention. Similarly, switching tabs frequently may be completely reasonable when a task requires research.

The personal baseline and Focus Insight provide additional context, but they do not change this fundamental limitation.

The formula may evolve in future versions as Focus Pulse develops more meaningful ways to represent browsing behaviour.

docs.title: Where the data lives
docs.text:
Each day is stored as a single small record in chrome.storage.local:

Field Contents sites Hostname → milliseconds of focused time switches Number of tab switches shortVisits Number of sessions under 10 seconds maxTabs Highest simultaneous tab count that day

Alongside these sits the in-progress session state — the current hostname and when its session started.

The daily records are used to calculate the focus score, 7-day trend, personal baseline, and Focus Insight.

The maxTabs value is tracked for informational purposes but is not currently used directly in the focus-score formula.

Because several listeners can fire at once — for example, a tab switch, tab close, and alarm — read-modify-write operations on the daily record are serialised through a queue. This prevents concurrent updates from overwriting each other and losing recorded activity.

Nothing here is transmitted anywhere. See Privacy for the full statement.

docs.title: From the Chrome Web Store
docs.text:
Focus Pulse is live on the Chrome Web Store. This is the recommended way to install it — Chrome keeps it updated for you.

Install from the Chrome Web Store

  1. Open the store listing.
  2. Click Add to Chrome, then confirm the permissions prompt.
  3. Pin the Focus Pulse icon to your toolbar so today's score is one click away.

The store package is built from this repository without modification, so the code you install is the code you can read here.

docs.title: Load unpacked (developers)
docs.text:
Focus Pulse has no build step. There is nothing to compile, bundle, or install — the repository is the extension.

  1. Clone the repository:
git clone https://github.com/Jainam249/browser-focus-tracker.git

  1. Open chrome://extensions in Chrome.

  2. Turn on Developer mode using the toggle in the top-right corner.

  3. Click Load unpacked.

  4. Select the cloned browser-focus-tracker folder.

Focus Pulse starts measuring immediately. Click the toolbar icon to view today's focus score, or open the dashboard from the popup to explore your focus history. The dashboard provides 7-day, 15-day and 30-day trend ranges, Bar Graph and Line Graph views, daily statistics, focus insights and a downloadable weekly report. Your selected graph type is remembered when you reopen the dashboard.

docs.title: Permissions you will be asked for
docs.text:
Chrome will list the permissions at install time. Each one is used entirely on your device — the privacy policy explains what each is for.

Permission Why tabs Read the active tab's hostname, count switches and open tabs storage Save your statistics locally idle Stop the clock when you step away alarms Checkpoint the session so Chrome's suspension doesn't lose it downloads Save exports to your Downloads folder when you ask

docs.title: Incognito
docs.text: Chrome does not run extensions in Incognito windows unless you explicitly allow it in chrome://extensions. Left at the default, Focus Pulse records nothing while you browse in Incognito.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text: Remove the extension from chrome://extensions. All of its stored data is deleted with it — there is no server-side copy, because there is no server.

docs.title: Privacy Policy
docs.text:
Focus Pulse · Chrome Extension Effective 20 August 2026 · Applies to version 1.0

Focus Pulse measures how you spend your own browsing time and shows it back to you. Every measurement it takes is stored on your computer, in your browser, and stays there. There is no server to send it to.

0network requests made by the extension 0third parties with access to your data Noaccount, login, or cloud sync Localstorage only, erased when you uninstall

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
• Focus Pulse records which website domain is in your active tab and for how long, so it can show you a daily focus score.
  • That information is written to your browser's local extension storage. It is never uploaded, transmitted, shared, or sold.
  • The extension contains no analytics, no tracking pixels, no advertising, and no code loaded from the internet.
  • Your data leaves your device only when you click an export button, and then it goes straight to your own Downloads folder.
  • Uninstalling the extension deletes everything it stored.

docs.title: What Focus Pulse stores on your device
docs.text:
For each calendar day, the extension keeps a small record in chrome.storage.local:

Site hostnames and time totals For example wikipedia.org paired with the number of milliseconds it was the focused tab. Only the hostname is kept, never the full address of the page. Tab switches A count of how many times you changed active tabs. Short visits A count of sessions that ended almost as soon as they started. Maximum open tabs The highest number of tabs open at once that day. Current session state The hostname you are on right now and when that session began, so a session survives Chrome suspending the extension. This is cleared each time the browser restarts.

These daily records accumulate locally to build the historical focus trends shown on the dashboard. The dashboard lets you view trends over 7-day, 15-day and 30-day ranges and switch between Bar Graph and Line Graph visualizations. These display options do not change what browsing data is collected or where it is stored. Nothing else is recorded.

docs.title: What it never touches
docs.text:
• The content of any page you visit. Focus Pulse injects no scripts into websites and cannot read them.
  • Full URLs, search queries, page titles, or paths. The address of the active tab is read only to extract the hostname, and is not retained.
  • Anything you type — keystrokes, form fields, passwords, messages.
  • Your name, email address, IP address, or any account identifier. The extension has no concept of who you are.
  • Your location, contacts, files, or download history.
  • Browser pages such as chrome://, edge://, about:, and extension pages, which are skipped entirely.

docs.title: Why each permission is requested
docs.text:
Focus Pulse asks for the smallest set of permissions that lets it measure attention. Every one of them is used entirely on your machine.

Permission What it is used for Leaves device? tabs Read the active tab's address to derive its hostname, count tab switches and open tabs, and detect whether a tab is playing audio so video time is not mistaken for idle time. No storage Save your statistics and in-progress session on your own device. Local storage only — never Chrome's account sync. No idle Notice when you step away or lock the screen, so time away from the computer is not counted as browsing. Only the coarse active / idle / locked state is read. No alarms Wake the extension once a minute to save the session in progress, so long stretches on one page are not lost when Chrome suspends it. No downloads Save the JSON, CSV, or weekly report file to your Downloads folder when you click an export button. The extension never downloads anything from the internet and does not read your existing downloads. Only if you export

docs.title: No remote code
docs.text: Everything Focus Pulse runs is included in the package you install from the Chrome Web Store. It loads no remote scripts, uses no eval() or dynamically constructed code, fetches no modules or WebAssembly at runtime, and contacts no server — because it does not have one.

docs.title: Sharing, selling, and analytics
docs.text: Focus Pulse does not sell or transfer your data to third parties. It does not use your data for advertising, credit or lending decisions, or any purpose unrelated to showing you your own focus statistics. There are no analytics or crash-reporting services embedded in it. Since nothing is transmitted, there is nothing to share.

docs.title: How long data is kept, and how to remove it
docs.text:
Daily records stay in your browser's local storage until you remove them. You are always in control:

Reset today The button in the extension popup deletes the current day's record immediately. Clear everything Removing Focus Pulse from chrome://extensions deletes all of its stored data along with it. Nothing survives elsewhere, because there is nowhere else. Take it with you Export your statistics as JSON or CSV at any time. The files are yours; the extension keeps no copy of what you exported.

docs.title: Incognito windows
docs.text: Chrome does not run extensions in Incognito windows unless you explicitly allow it. Left at the default, Focus Pulse records nothing while you browse in Incognito.

docs.title: Children
docs.text: Focus Pulse is not directed at children and collects no personal information from anyone, regardless of age.

docs.title: Changes to this policy
docs.text: If a future version of Focus Pulse changes what it measures or stores, this page will be updated and the effective date at the top revised before that version is published. A change that introduced any transmission of your data off your device would be stated here plainly.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Questions about this policy, or about the extension's handling of data, can be sent to sjainam141@gmail.com. This is the same address verified as the publisher contact on the Chrome Web Store listing.
